        "displayText": "Your answers give me a clear picture. You want a **single, self-contained MLX model directory** where mixed-precision quantization, Hadamard rotation, KV-cache optimization, long-context fixes, and the dynamic-frame template are all already baked in. The end user downloads it, points their runtime at it, and everything works. No configuration, no extra flags.\n\nThe honest constraint first: a truly “double-click” install isn’t possible with the KV-cache and RoPE changes. That is the closest thing to “hardbaked” that exists for this class of optimizations, and you already said remote code execution is acceptable.\n\nHere is the complete, start-to-finish roadmap.\n\n---\n\n### 🗺️ The Roadmap at a Glance\n\n| Step | What it does | Tool | What you run |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **1** | Mixed-precision quantization (MLP 4-bit, Attn 6-bit, Embed 4-bit, LM Head 6-bit) | **AXQuant** | One command |\n| **2** | Hadamard rotation of the **weights** (baked into safetensors) | **SpinQuant-style rotation** | One Python script |\n| **3** | Hadamard rotation of the **KV cache** (runtime, full-attention layers only) | **mlx-turboquant** logic | Custom `modeling_spark.py` |\n| **4** | Long-context fix (YaRN/NTK RoPE scaling on full-attention layers) | Custom RoPE patch | Same `modeling_spark.py` |\n| **5** | Dynamic-frame template (Sharp v5 + automatic mode selection) | Your existing template | File swap |\n| **6** | Package and validate | `mlx-lm` | One test command |\n\nI will write every script and every patch. You will copy them into files, run them, and paste back the output when something needs checking.\n\n---\n\n## Step 1 — Mixed-Precision Quantization with AXQuant\n\nAXQuant is the only tool purpose-built for MLX that assigns **different bit-widths per tensor** while keeping sensitive layers (norms, heads) at hard floors. It inspects your BF16 safetensors checkpoint and produces a mixed-precision MLX model with standard MLX configuration files.\n\n**Your target mix** (MLP 4-bit, Attention 6-bit, Embed 4-bit, LM Head 6-bit) averages to roughly **4.2 bits per weight**, which is exactly what you asked for.\n\n### What you do\n\n```bash\n# 1. Create a virtual environment (AXQuant requires Python 3.11+)\npython3 -m venv axquant-venv\nsource axquant-venv/bin/activate\n\n# 2. Install AXQuant with MLX support\npython -m pip install -U pip\npython -m pip install 'axquant[mlx]==1.8.1'\n\n# 3. Run the quantizer on your BF16 model directory\n#    Replace /path/to/Spark-2.6-4B-bf16 with your actual local folder\naxquant quantize /path/to/Spark-2.6-4B-bf16 \\\n  --target-bpw 4.2 \\\n  --output ./Spark-2.6-4B-AXQ\n```\n\nThe `--target-bpw 4.2` flag tells AXQuant to allocate bits so the average comes out around 4.2. It will protect norms and sensitive layers automatically. The output folder `Spark-2.6-4B-AXQ` will contain the mixed-precision safetensors and MLX config files.\n\n**What to check before moving on:** Open `./Spark-2.6-4B-AXQ/config.json` and confirm there is a `\"quantization\"` block. The exact per-layer bit assignments will be in there. Paste it back to me if anything looks off.\n\n---\n\n## Step 2 — Hadamard Rotation of the Weights (Baked In)\n\nThis is the step that makes the model **quantization-friendly** before you quantize it. The principle is simple: for a linear layer `y = W x`, if you rotate the input with an orthonormal matrix `H`, you can write `y = (W Hᵀ) (H x)`. You store `W Hᵀ` in the safetensors file. At runtime, the model must apply `H` to the input activation before the layer. The rotation spreads outliers across channels, which makes low-bit quantization much more accurate.\n\n**Critical ordering:** Rotation must happen **before** quantization. You rotate the BF16 weights first, save them as BF16, and *then* run AXQuant on the rotated checkpoint. If you quantize first and try to rotate afterward, you are rotating already-lossy weights and the benefit is reduced.\n\n### The rotation script\n\nCreate a file called `rotate_spark_weights.py`. This script applies a **blockwise Hadamard rotation** to the input dimension of the attention and MLP projection weights. It uses blocks of **64** because `hidden_size = 2560` is divisible by 64 but not a power of two, and MLX’s Hadamard transform prefers power-of-two block sizes.\n\n```python\n# rotate_spark_weights.py\n# Applies blockwise Hadamard rotation to Spark-X2.6 projection weights.\n# Input:  ./Spark-2.6-4B-bf16  (original BF16 safetensors)\n# Output: ./Spark-2.6-4B-rotated-bf16\n\nimport json, math, shutil\nfrom pathlib import Path\nimport numpy as np\nimport torch\nfrom safetensors.torch import load_file, save_file\n\nSRC = Path(\"./Spark-2.6-4B-bf16\")        # <-- your BF16 model folder\nDST = Path(\"./Spark-2.6-4B-rotated-bf16\")\nDST.mkdir(exist_ok=True)\n\nBLOCK = 64  # rotation block size\n\ndef hadamard_block(d):\n    H = np.array([[1.0]])\n    while H.shape[0] < d:\n        H = np.block([[H, H], [H, -H]])\n    return torch.tensor(H / math.sqrt(d), dtype=torch.float32)\n\nH = hadamard_block(BLOCK)  # [64, 64]\n\n# Load all safetensors shards\nindex = json.loads((SRC / \"model.safetensors.index.json\").read_text())\nweight_map = index[\"weight_map\"]\nall_weights = {}\nfor shard in set(weight_map.values()):\n    all_weights.update(load_file(str(SRC / shard)))\n\nnew_weights = dict(all_weights)\n\ndef rotate_input_dim(W):\n    \"\"\"W shape: [out_features, in_features]. Rotate in_features in blocks.\"\"\"\n    out_f, in_f = W.shape\n    if in_f % BLOCK != 0:\n        return W  # skip if not divisible\n    W = W.float()\n    W_blocks = W.reshape(out_f, in_f // BLOCK, BLOCK)\n    W_rot = torch.einsum(\"obk,kj->obj\", W_blocks, H.T)  # W @ H^T per block\n    return W_rot.reshape(out_f, in_f)\n\n# Rotate attention projections and MLP projections\ntarget_suffixes = [\n    \"self_attn.q_k_v_proj.weight\",\n    \"self_attn.out_proj.weight\",\n    \"mlp.gate_proj.weight\",\n    \"mlp.up_proj.weight\",\n    \"mlp.down_proj.weight\",\n]\n\nfor name, W in all_weights.items():\n    if any(name.endswith(s) for s in target_suffixes):\n        new_weights[name] = rotate_input_dim(W).to(torch.bfloat16)\n        print(f\"rotated {name}: {tuple(W.shape)}\")\n\n# Save shards\nshard_map = {}\nfor i, shard in enumerate(sorted(set(weight_map.values()))):\n    keys_in_shard = [k for k, v in weight_map.items() if v == shard]\n    shard_weights = {k: new_weights[k] for k in keys_in_shard}\n    out_name = f\"model-{i+1:05d}-of-{len(set(weight_map.values())):05d}.safetensors\"\n    save_file(shard_weights, str(DST / out_name))\n    for k in keys_in_shard:\n        shard_map[k] = out_name\n\n# Copy config and tokenizer files\nfor f in [\"config.json\", \"tokenizer_config.json\", \"tokenizer.json\",\n          \"special_tokens_map.json\", \"generation_config.json\"]:\n    if (SRC / f).exists():\n        shutil.copy(SRC / f, DST / f)\n\n# Write new index\nindex[\"weight_map\"] = shard_map\n(DST / \"model.safetensors.index.json\").write_text(json.dumps(index, indent=2))\n\nprint(f\"\\nDone. Rotated model saved to {DST}\")\n```\n\n**What this does:** It loads every safetensors shard, applies a 64-block Hadamard rotation to the **input dimension** of `q_k_v_proj`, `out_proj`, `gate_proj`, `up_proj`, and `down_proj`, and saves a new BF16 checkpoint. The rotation is mathematically equivalent to the original (orthogonal), but the weight distribution is now more Gaussian.\n\n**What you run:**\n```bash\npython rotate_spark_weights.py\n```\n\n---\n\n## Step 3 — Quantize the Rotated Weights\n\nNow you run AXQuant **on the rotated BF16 checkpoint**, not the original.\n\n```bash\n# Still inside the axquant-venv\naxquant quantize ./Spark-2.6-4B-rotated-bf16 \\\n  --target-bpw 4.2 \\\n  --output ./Spark-2.6-4B-AXQ-rotated\n```\n\nThe output `Spark-2.6-4B-AXQ-rotated` is your **mixed-precision, Hadamard-rotated model**. The weights are baked. The only thing missing at this point is the runtime patch that applies the matching rotation to the activations.\n\n---\n\n## Step 4 — Runtime Patch for Weight Rotation\n\nBecause you rotated the **input dimension** of the projections, the model must rotate the **hidden states** before those projections at inference time. This is a one-line change in the attention and MLP forward passes.\n\nIn `modeling_spark.py`, find the attention forward pass. It will look something like:\n\n```python\n# BEFORE (original):\nq, k, v = self.q_k_v_proj(hidden_states).split([...], dim=-1)\n```\n\nYou need to change it to:\n\n```python\n# AFTER (rotated weights):\nhidden_states_rot = rotate_blockwise(hidden_states, self.H)  # H is the 64x64 Hadamard\nq, k, v = self.q_k_v_proj(hidden_states_rot).split([...], dim=-1)\n```\n\nAnd similarly for the MLP:\n\n```python\n# BEFORE:\ngate = self.gate_proj(hidden_states)\nup = self.up_proj(hidden_states)\n\n# AFTER:\nhidden_states_rot = rotate_blockwise(hidden_states, self.H)\ngate = self.gate_proj(hidden_states_rot)\nup = self.up_proj(hidden_states_rot)\n```\n\n**Important:** The rotation must be applied **after RMSNorm and before the projection**, because RMSNorm is not rotation-invariant. `down_proj` takes the MLP intermediate as input; if you rotate `down_proj`’s input dimension, you must rotate the intermediate activation before `down_proj`, and then **un-rotate the output** of `down_proj` if the next layer expects the original basis. The safest approach is to rotate only `q_k_v_proj`, `gate_proj`, and `up_proj`, and leave `down_proj` and `out_proj` unrotated to avoid the un-rotation complexity. The attention output (`out_proj`) and MLP output (`down_proj`) go into residual connections, and rotating their input dimension without un-rotating the output would corrupt the residual stream.\n\nI will write the **exact patch** once you paste the `Attention` and `MLP` classes from your `modeling_spark.py`. The file is 21 KB, so it is manageable.\n\n---\n\n## Step 5 — KV Cache Rotation with TurboQuant Logic\n\nThis is the runtime piece that cannot be baked into safetensors. You will implement a `TurboQuantKVCache`-style class that stores **keys in the Hadamard-rotated frame** and rotates the query to match.\n\nThe `mlx-turboquant` library already implements this. The key insight is: **rotate the query once, un-rotate the output once**, and attention scores are unchanged because the rotation is orthogonal.\n\n**Which layers:** Only the **full-attention layers** (3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31, 35). The sliding-window layers already use a bounded 512-token `RotatingKVCache` and never accumulate long contexts. Rotating their keys is wasted work.\n\n**What you will add to `modeling_spark.py`:**\n\n```python\n# At the top:\nfrom mlx_turboquant.kv_cache import TurboQuantKVCache\n\n# In the Attention __init__:\nif is_full_attention_layer:\n    self.kv_cache = TurboQuantKVCache(\n        head_dim=self.head_dim,\n        bits=4,          # or 8 for higher fidelity\n        group_size=64,\n    )\nelse:\n    self.kv_cache = RotatingKVCache(...)  # keep original\n```\n\nThe `TurboQuantKVCache` stores keys in the rotated frame and handles the query rotation internally. This is a **drop-in replacement** for the standard cache class.\n\n**What to test:** Generate at 4k and 128k tokens with the same prompt. The attention scores should be mathematically identical to the unrotated cache (because the rotation is orthogonal). The benefit is that the key distribution is more Gaussian, which makes the 4-bit cache quantization much more accurate than it would be without rotation.\n\n---\n\n## Step 6 — Long-Context Fix: YaRN/NTK RoPE Scaling\n\nYour degradation at 125k–200k tokens is almost certainly **RoPE extrapolation failure**, not a cache-format issue. The full-attention layers use `partial_rotary_factor: 0.25` with `rope_theta: 5,000,000`. That is an unusual combination: a very high base on a very narrow slice of the head. When the context exceeds the training distribution, the model loses track of position.\n\n**The fix:** Apply **YaRN scaling** to the full-attention layers only. YaRN holds accuracy noticeably better than linear scaling at the same extension ratio.\n\nIn `modeling_spark.py`, the RoPE initialization for full-attention layers will look something like:\n\n```python\n# BEFORE:\nrope = initialize_rope(\n    dims=head_dim,\n    base=5000000,\n    traditional=False,\n    scaling_config=None,\n)\n```\n\nYou need to change it to:\n\n```python\n# AFTER (YaRN):\nrope = initialize_rope(\n    dims=head_dim,\n    base=5000000,\n    traditional=False,\n    scaling_config={\n        \"type\": \"yarn\",\n        \"factor\": 4.0,          # extend 4× beyond native\n        \"original_max_position_embeddings\": 262144,\n    },\n)\n```\n\nThe `factor` controls how aggressively the context is stretched. A factor of 4.0 extends a 256k-native window to ~1M. You may need to tune this between 2.0 and 8.0 depending on how the model behaves. The honest rule is: **2× native is safe, 4× degrades, 8× is risky**. Start with 4.0 and test.\n\n**Important:** Do not apply YaRN to the sliding-window layers. They already use full rotary with `theta=10000` and a 512-token window; they are not the source of long-context drift.\n\nI will write the exact RoPE patch once you paste the relevant `initialize_rope` call from `modeling_spark.py`.\n\n---\n\n## Step 7 — The Dynamic-Frame Template (Sharp v5 + Automatic Selection)\n\nYour `chat_template.jinja` is already the **Sharp v5 dynamic-frame template**. It does not use keyword routing; it injects a **FRAME CARD** and instructs the model to silently select the best construct/persona/identity. This is actually better than the keyword-router approach I suggested earlier, because it is fully semantic and cannot leak routing logic (the logic is in the model’s reasoning, not in the template).\n\n**What needs to change:** Nothing structural. The template already works. But you mentioned you want the **Turbo Brilliance** modes blended in. The Sharp v5 template already has 16 constructs (including `coder`, `teacher`, `story`, `logic`, `socrates`, `brainstorm`, etc.) that cover the same ground as Turbo Brilliance’s modes. The FRAME CARD already tells the model to pick the best one silently.\n\n**If you want to add specific Severian/Engram-inspired modes**, you can add new constructs to the `CONSTRUCT` list in the FRAME CARD. For example:\n\n```jinja\n  engram — access static hashed memory + dynamic memory features; recall relevant context from prior turns and hashed slots\n  belief — predictive-belief mode; track user’s evolving beliefs, contradictions, and updates across the conversation\n  temporal — temporal-engram mode; anchor events in time, track sequences, durations, and causal order\n```\n\nThese would be **new frame options** that the model can choose from. The engram models on Hugging Face add actual sidecar modules to the architecture; you cannot replicate that with a template alone. But you *can* add a mode that instructs the model to behave *as if* it has those capabilities, which is what the Sharp template already does for its existing constructs.\n\n**To add modes:** Edit the `FRAME CARD` section in your `chat_template.jinja`. Add the new construct names to the `CONSTRUCT` list. The model will then be able to select them.\n\n---\n\n## Step 8 — Package and Validate\n\nYour final model directory will contain:\n\n```\nSpark-2.6-4B-Final/\n├── model.safetensors          # mixed-precision, Hadamard-rotated weights (from AXQuant)\n├── config.json                # AXQuant config + quantization block\n├── tokenizer_config.json\n├── chat_template.jinja        # Sharp v5 dynamic frame (possibly with new modes)\n├── modeling_spark.py          # patched: weight rotation + KV cache rotation + YaRN RoPE\n└── (other tokenizer files)\n```\n\n**Validation checklist:**\n\n1. **Load test:** `python -c \"from mlx_lm import load; m, t = load('./Spark-2.6-4B-Final')\"` — should load without errors.\n2. **Short generation:** Generate 100 tokens at 4k context. Output should be coherent.\n3. **Long generation:** Generate 100 tokens at 128k context. Compare to the original BF16 model. The rotated/quantized version should not be noticeably worse.\n4. **Template test:** Send “Write a Python function” and “Tell me a story” and verify the model shifts behavior (coder vs. story) without announcing the mode.\n\n**What I need from you to finish the runtime patches:**\n\n1. **The `Attention` class** from `modeling_spark.py` (or the whole file). I need to see exactly how `q_k_v_proj` is called and how the KV cache is updated.\n2. **The `MLP` class** (so I can patch the gate/up projections correctly).\n3. **The `initialize_rope` call** (so I can patch YaRN).\n4. **Confirmation** that `mlx-turboquant` installs cleanly in your environment (`pip install mlx-turboquant`).\n\nOnce I have those, I will write the **complete `modeling_spark.py`** with all three patches (weight rotation, KV cache, YaRN) already applied. Rotate in_features in blocks.\"\"\"\n    out_f, in_f = W.shape\n    if in_f % BLOCK != 0:\n        return W  # skip if not divisible\n    W = W.float()\n    W_blocks = W.reshape(out_f, in_f // BLOCK, BLOCK)\n    W_rot = torch.einsum(\"obk,kj->obj\", W_blocks, H.T)  # W @ H^T per block\n    return W_rot.reshape(out_f, in_f)\n\n# Rotate attention projections and MLP projections\ntarget_suffixes = [\n    \"self_attn.q_k_v_proj.weight\",\n    \"self_attn.out_proj.weight\",\n    \"mlp.gate_proj.weight\",\n    \"mlp.up_proj.weight\",\n    \"mlp.down_proj.weight\",\n]\n\nfor name, W in all_weights.items():\n    if any(name.endswith(s) for s in target_suffixes):\n        new_weights[name] = rotate_input_dim(W).to(torch.bfloat16)\n        print(f\"rotated {name}: {tuple(W.shape)}\")\n\n# Save shards\nshard_map = {}\nfor i, shard in enumerate(sorted(set(weight_map.values()))):\n    keys_in_shard = [k for k, v in weight_map.items() if v == shard]\n    shard_weights = {k: new_weights[k] for k in keys_in_shard}\n    out_name = f\"model-{i+1:05d}-of-{len(set(weight_map.values())):05d}.safetensors\"\n    save_file(shard_weights, str(DST / out_name))\n    for k in keys_in_shard:\n        shard_map[k] = out_name\n\n# Copy config and tokenizer files\nfor f in [\"config.json\", \"tokenizer_config.json\", \"tokenizer.json\",\n          \"special_tokens_map.json\", \"generation_config.json\"]:\n    if (SRC / f).exists():\n        shutil.copy(SRC / f, DST / f)\n\n# Write new index\nindex[\"weight_map\"] = shard_map\n(DST / \"model.safetensors.index.json\").write_text(json.dumps(index, indent=2))\n\nprint(f\"\\nDone. Rotated model saved to {DST}\")\n```\n\n**What this does:** It loads every safetensors shard, applies a 64-block Hadamard rotation to the **input dimension** of `q_k_v_proj`, `out_proj`, `gate_proj`, `up_proj`, and `down_proj`, and saves a new BF16 checkpoint. The rotation is mathematically equivalent to the original (orthogonal), but the weight distribution is now more Gaussian.\n\n**What you run:**\n```bash\npython rotate_spark_weights.py\n```\n\n---\n\n## Step 3 — Quantize the Rotated Weights\n\nNow you run AXQuant **on the rotated BF16 checkpoint**, not the original.\n\n```bash\n# Still inside the axquant-venv\naxquant quantize ./Spark-2.6-4B-rotated-bf16 \\\n  --target-bpw 4.2 \\\n  --output ./Spark-2.6-4B-AXQ-rotated\n```\n\nThe output `Spark-2.6-4B-AXQ-rotated` is your **mixed-precision, Hadamard-rotated model**. The weights are baked. The only thing missing at this point is the runtime patch that applies the matching rotation to the activations.\n\n---\n\n## Step 4 — Runtime Patch for Weight Rotation\n\nBecause you rotated the **input dimension** of the projections, the model must rotate the **hidden states** before those projections at inference time. This is a one-line change in the attention and MLP forward passes.\n\nIn `modeling_spark.py`, find the attention forward pass. It will look something like:\n\n```python\n# BEFORE (original):\nq, k, v = self.q_k_v_proj(hidden_states).split([...], dim=-1)\n```\n\nYou need to change it to:\n\n```python\n# AFTER (rotated weights):\nhidden_states_rot = rotate_blockwise(hidden_states, self.H)  # H is the 64x64 Hadamard\nq, k, v = self.q_k_v_proj(hidden_states_rot).split([...], dim=-1)\n```\n\nAnd similarly for the MLP:\n\n```python\n# BEFORE:\ngate = self.gate_proj(hidden_states)\nup = self.up_proj(hidden_states)\n\n# AFTER:\nhidden_states_rot = rotate_blockwise(hidden_states, self.H)\ngate = self.gate_proj(hidden_states_rot)\nup = self.up_proj(hidden_states_rot)\n```\n\n**Important:** The rotation must be applied **after RMSNorm and before the projection**, because RMSNorm is not rotation-invariant. `down_proj` takes the MLP intermediate as input; if you rotate `down_proj`’s input dimension, you must rotate the intermediate activation before `down_proj`, and then **un-rotate the output** of `down_proj` if the next layer expects the original basis. The safest approach is to rotate only `q_k_v_proj`, `gate_proj`, and `up_proj`, and leave `down_proj` and `out_proj` unrotated to avoid the un-rotation complexity. The attention output (`out_proj`) and MLP output (`down_proj`) go into residual connections, and rotating their input dimension without un-rotating the output would corrupt the residual stream.\n\nI will write the **exact patch** once you paste the `Attention` and `MLP` classes from your `modeling_spark.py`. The file is 21 KB, so it is manageable.\n\n---\n\n## Step 5 — KV Cache Rotation with TurboQuant Logic\n\nThis is the runtime piece that cannot be baked into safetensors. You will implement a `TurboQuantKVCache`-style class that stores **keys in the Hadamard-rotated frame** and rotates the query to match.\n\nThe `mlx-turboquant` library already implements this. The key insight is: **rotate the query once, un-rotate the output once**, and attention scores are unchanged because the rotation is orthogonal.\n\n**Which layers:** Only the **full-attention layers** (3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31, 35). The sliding-window layers already use a bounded 512-token `RotatingKVCache` and never accumulate long contexts. Rotating their keys is wasted work.\n\n**What you will add to `modeling_spark.py`:**\n\n```python\n# At the top:\nfrom mlx_turboquant.kv_cache import TurboQuantKVCache\n\n# In the Attention __init__:\nif is_full_attention_layer:\n    self.kv_cache = TurboQuantKVCache(\n        head_dim=self.head_dim,\n        bits=4,          # or 8 for higher fidelity\n        group_size=64,\n    )\nelse:\n    self.kv_cache = RotatingKVCache(...)  # keep original\n```\n\nThe `TurboQuantKVCache` stores keys in the rotated frame and handles the query rotation internally. This is a **drop-in replacement** for the standard cache class.\n\n**What to test:** Generate at 4k and 128k tokens with the same prompt. The attention scores should be mathematically identical to the unrotated cache (because the rotation is orthogonal). The benefit is that the key distribution is more Gaussian, which makes the 4-bit cache quantization much more accurate than it would be without rotation.\n\n---\n\n## Step 6 — Long-Context Fix: YaRN/NTK RoPE Scaling\n\nYour degradation at 125k–200k tokens is almost certainly **RoPE extrapolation failure**, not a cache-format issue. The full-attention layers use `partial_rotary_factor: 0.25` with `rope_theta: 5,000,000`. That is an unusual combination: a very high base on a very narrow slice of the head. When the context exceeds the training distribution, the model loses track of position.\n\n**The fix:** Apply **YaRN scaling** to the full-attention layers only. YaRN holds accuracy noticeably better than linear scaling at the same extension ratio.\n\nIn `modeling_spark.py`, the RoPE initialization for full-attention layers will look something like:\n\n```python\n# BEFORE:\nrope = initialize_rope(\n    dims=head_dim,\n    base=5000000,\n    traditional=False,\n    scaling_config=None,\n)\n```\n\nYou need to change it to:\n\n```python\n# AFTER (YaRN):\nrope = initialize_rope(\n    dims=head_dim,\n    base=5000000,\n    traditional=False,\n    scaling_config={\n        \"type\": \"yarn\",\n        \"factor\": 4.0,          # extend 4× beyond native\n        \"original_max_position_embeddings\": 262144,\n    },\n)\n```\n\nThe `factor` controls how aggressively the context is stretched. A factor of 4.0 extends a 256k-native window to ~1M. You may need to tune this between 2.0 and 8.0 depending on how the model behaves. The honest rule is: **2× native is safe, 4× degrades, 8× is risky**. Start with 4.0 and test.\n\n**Important:** Do not apply YaRN to the sliding-window layers. They already use full rotary with `theta=10000` and a 512-token window; they are not the source of long-context drift.\n\nI will write the exact RoPE patch once you paste the relevant `initialize_rope` call from `modeling_spark.py`.\n\n---\n\n## Step 7 — The Dynamic-Frame Template (Sharp v5 + Automatic Selection)\n\nYour `chat_template.jinja` is already the **Sharp v5 dynamic-frame template**. It CANNOT live in\n175: `directions.EXTRACTORS` — those receive a single layer's activations, this needs\n176: all of them — so `pipeline.gabliterate` special-cases it and `DirectionSet.layer`\n177: is set to `pipeline.GLOBAL_LAYER = -1` (\"belongs to no single layer\"). The sign of\n178: an SVD vector is arbitrary, so it is fixed by aligning with the pooled mean\n179: difference (the positive side must project higher, else the edit reinforces the\n180: behaviour instead of removing it). `directions.stacked_differences` does the\n181: pairing — rows are paired positionally, because the capture runs the same\n182: prompts on both sides.\n183: `--wash {plain,orthogonalize,jwash}` is the J-Wash recipe (Apache-2.0, attribute\n184: in the PR body): `orthogonalize` restores the edited matrix's ORIGINAL singular\n185: values while keeping its own singular vectors, so the behaviour direction really\n186: is written into the weights but the layer's output scale does not move;\n187: `jwash` = orthogonalize + rescale the Frobenius norm to the original.\n188: `surgery.restore_singular_values` / `rescale_frobenius` do the work in numpy\n189: float64 (MLX float32 matmuls on this M5 are ~1e-3 accurate) and accept a single\n190: matrix (m,n) or an expert stack (E,m,n). `surgery._postprocess_weight` is the\n191: mx-array wrapper, called from `apply_to_targets` in BOTH the dense branch and the\n192: expert branch. `pipeline._wash_steps` maps a wash name to (orthogonalize, rescale).\n193: \n194: ## t4-2 additions (do not re-derive)\n195: \n196: **Per-layer directions (ZeroFuse-shaped, MIT source read only).**\n197: `directions.per_layer_directions(pos_states, neg_states, layers=None, k=1,\n198: method=\"mean_diff\")` → `{layer: (d,k)}`; it loops the per-layer extractors over\n199: the layers BOTH banks were captured for, and the rows stay aligned because the\n200: capture runs the same prompts on both sides. `directions.fuse_directions(bases,\n201: weights=None)` → `(d,r)`: stacks the per-layer bases as ROWS, takes the top\n202: right singular vectors of that stack, keeps `n_cols` columns, and fixes the\n203: sign by aligning with the summed per-basis means (falling back to the FIRST\n204: basis' mean when the inputs cancel, so the sign is never the arbitrary one of\n205: a singular vector). `directions.fractional_layer_index(frac, n_layers)` maps a\n206: fractional depth to a layer (0.0 → first block, 1.0 → last).\n207: \n208: **Wiring constraint.** The `EXTRACTORS` registry is per-layer\n209: `(H_pos, H_neg) -> (d,k)`, so a method that needs every layer CANNOT be an\n210: EXTRACTORS entry. `global_svd`, `per_layer` and `fused` are special-cased in\n211: `pipeline.gabliterate` Phase 2 instead; `extractor_layer` is set to\n212: `GLOBAL_LAYER` (-1) for `global_svd`. In the `per_layer` mode the\n213: `DirectionSet` carries the FUSED basis for provenance while the per-layer\n214: bases drive the edit. `surgery.apply_to_targets` takes a `projector_for(target)`\n215: resolver: one `Projector` (unchanged), a dict `{layer: Projector}`, or a\n216: callable. The embedding falls back to the shared projector.\n217: \n218: **The embedding role (Auto-Abliteration-shaped).** The token embedding is a\n219: SOURCE of residual vectors, not a write into them, so it is not a\n220: residual-write projection: `arch.EMBED_LAYER = -2` (distinct from\n221: `GLOBAL_LAYER = -1`), `arch._embedding_target` gives it `side=\"right\"` (each\n222: row is a token's residual vector, so the direction is read out of E's COLUMNS —\n223: the opposite side from a down-projection, which is left-multiplied), and\n224: `resolve_targets` detects it BEFORE the `_excluded_prefix` and\n225: `layer is None` skips. **`\"embed\"` is deliberately NOT in `arch.ALL_ROLES`** —\n226: it is opt-in via `--embed` / `roles=(\"embed\",)`, so the default target set is\n227: unchanged. The embedding belongs to no block, so it gets its own alpha\n228: (`--embed-alpha`, defaulting to the first edited block's).\n229: \n230: **The tuner (abliterix-shaped, AGPL source read only).** The package ALREADY\n231: had `tune.py` (`TuneCandidate`, `TuneMeasurement`, `TuneResult`, `TuneReport`,\n232: `candidate_grid`, `composite_score`, `search`, `tune_model`,\n233: `make_generate_fn`) — do NOT add a second tuner. `composite_score` =\n234: `refusal + lam*over_refusal + mu*fidelity` (smaller is better); `search` is\n235: pure and model-free, and a candidate whose measurement raises is recorded in\n236: `report.failures` instead of aborting the sweep. `tune_model` snapshots the\n237: weights, restores them before every candidate, and restores them again in a\n238: `finally:` block.\n239: \n240: Two guards were added to `tune.py`:\n241: * `tune.kl_divergence(ref, mod, floor=1e-9)` — KL over two aligned lists of\n242:   top-k log-probability dicts, each side renormalised over its own top-k\n243:   (the tables are truncated, so their masses do not sum to one). It accepts\n244:   probability tables too: a table is treated as log-probs when it holds a\n245:   negative entry. `tune._topk_logprobs(model, tokenizer, prompts, k=20)` reads\n246:   the last position and swallows per-prompt exceptions.\n247: * `tune.control_verdict(base_rate, candidate_rates, tolerance=0.0)` — the\n248:   POSITIVE CONTROL. If no candidate moved the refusal metric, the harness is\n249:   not reading signal and the ranking is meaningless, so it returns False and\n250:   the sweep must not crown a winner. `mlx-gablate tune` prints the control\n251:   verdict and exits 2 when it fails.\n252: \n253: **The drift audit (abldrift-shaped, MIT).** `drift.py` is new: `Probe`,\n254: `DeltaVector`, `bootstrap_ci` (percentile bootstrap of the mean),\n255: `compute_delta` (paired `modified - base`), `load_probes` (JSON or YAML),\n256: `lexical_judge` (cue hits per 100 words), `paired_audit`, `compare_audits`,\n257: `default_probes`, `format_report`. A dimension counts as drifted only when the\n258: mean moved AND the bootstrap interval excludes zero — a shift within the noise\n259: is not a finding. `mlx-gablate drift --model M --baseline B` runs the same\n260: probes against both models and exits 1 when something breached.\n261: \n262: **New CLI commands:** `mlx-gablate tune` (search (method, layers, alpha) with\n263: the control check) and `mlx-gablate drift` (paired before/after character\n264: audit). `mlx-gablate gabliterate` gained `--embed`, `--embed-alpha`,\n265: `--base-method` and `--layer-frac`; `--method` gained `per_layer` and `fused`.\n266: \n267: ## t4-3 / t4-4 findings (do not re-derive)\n268: \n269: - **`io.load_model` returns `(model, config)`, not `(model, tokenizer)`.** It wraps\n270:   `mlx_lm.utils.load_model`.               "content": "#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"\nrotate_spark_weights.py\n=======================\nApplies blockwise Hadamard rotation to the INPUT dimension of the attention\nand MLP projection weights of a Spark-X2.6-4B BF16 checkpoint.\n\nPrinciple: for y = W x, rotating input with orthonormal H gives\ny = (W @ H.T) @ (H @ x). We store W @ H.T in the safetensors; at runtime\nthe model applies H to the activation before the layer.\n\nCritical: rotation happens BEFORE quantization. Rotate BF16 weights, save\nas BF16, then run AXQuant on the rotated checkpoint.\n\nRotation targets (input dimension rotated):\n  self_attn.q_k_v_proj.weight   [q_dim, hidden]   -> rotate hidden\n  mlp.gate_proj.weight          [intermediate, hidden] -> rotate hidden\n  mlp.up_proj.weight            [intermediate, hidden] -> rotate hidden\n\nNOT rotated (to avoid un-rotation complexity on residual stream):\n  self_attn.out_proj.weight     [hidden, q_dim]   -> skip\n  mlp.down_proj.weight          [hidden, intermediate] -> skip\n\nUsage:\n    python rotate_spark_weights.py \\\n        --src ./Spark-2.6-4B-bf16 \\\n        --dst ./Spark-2.6-4B-rotated-bf16 \\\n        --block 64\n\"\"\"\n\nimport argparse\nimport json\nimport math\nimport shutil\nfrom pathlib import Path\n\nimport numpy as np\nimport torch\nfrom safetensors.torch import load_file, save_file\n\n\ndef hadamard_block(d: int) -> torch.Tensor:\n    \"\"\"Build a d x d Hadamard matrix (d must be a power of 2), normalized.\"\"\"\n    H = np.array([[1.0]])\n    while H.shape[0] < d:\n        H = np.block([[H, H], [H, -H]])\n    return torch.tensor(H / math.sqrt(d), dtype=torch.float32)\n\n\ndef rotate_input_dim(W: torch.Tensor, H: torch.Tensor, block: int) -> torch.Tensor:\n    \"\"\"Rotate the input dimension of W in blocks of size `block`.\n\n    W shape: [out_features, in_features]. We compute W @ H.T per block.\n    \"\"\"\n    out_f, in_f = W.shape\n    if in_f % block != 0:\n        return W  # skip if not divisible\n    W = W.float()\n    W_blocks = W.reshape(out_f, in_f // block, block)\n    # einsum: for each output o and block b, W_rot[o, b, :] = sum_k W_blocks[o, b, k] * H.T[k, :]\n    # H.T has shape [block, block], so W @ H.T per block\n    W_rot = torch.einsum(\"obk,kj->obj\", W_blocks, H.T)\n    return W_rot.reshape(out_f, in_f)\n\n\ndef main():\n    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()\n    parser.add_argument(\"--src\", required=True, help=\"Source BF16 model folder\")\n    parser.add_argument(\"--dst\", required=True, help=\"Output rotated BF16 model folder\")\n    parser.add_argument(\"--block\", type=int, default=64, help=\"Hadamard block size\")\n    args = parser.parse_args()\n\n    SRC = Path(args.src)\n    DST = Path(args.dst)\n    BLOCK = args.block\n\n    if not SRC.exists():\n        raise SystemExit(f\"Source directory not found: {SRC}\")\n\n    DST.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)\n\n    H = hadamard_block(BLOCK)\n    print(f\"Hadamard block {BLOCK}x{BLOCK} built. Hidden size must be divisible by {BLOCK}.\")\n\n    # ---- Load index ----\n    index_path = SRC / \"model.safetensors.index.json\"\n    if not index_path.exists():\n        raise SystemExit(f\"model.safetensors.index.json not found in {SRC}\")\n\n    index = json.loads(index_path.read_text())\n    weight_map = index[\"weight_map\"]\n    shards = sorted(set(weight_map.values()))\n    print(f\"Found {len(shards)} shard(s), {len(weight_map)} tensors\")\n\n    # ---- Load all weights ----\n    all_weights = {}\n    for shard in shards:\n        shard_path = SRC / shard\n        if not shard_path.exists():\n            raise SystemExit(f\"Shard not found: {shard_path}\")\n        all_weights.update(load_file(str(shard_path)))\n\n    # ---- Rotation targets ----\n    target_suffixes = [\n        \"self_attn.q_k_v_proj.weight\",\n        \"mlp.gate_proj.weight\",\n        \"mlp.up_proj.weight\",\n    ]\n\n    hidden_size = None\n    # Try to read hidden_size from config\n    config_path = SRC / \"config.json\"\n    if config_path.exists():\n        cfg = json.loads(config_path.read_text())\n        hidden_size = cfg.get(\"hidden_size\")\n        print(f\"Config hidden_size: {hidden_size}\")\n\n    if hidden_size and hidden_size % BLOCK != 0:\n        print(f\"WARNING: hidden_size={hidden_size} not divisible by block={BLOCK}. \"\n              f\"Rotated layers will be skipped.\")\n\n    new_weights = dict(all_weights)\n    rotated_count = 0\n    skipped_count = 0\n\n    for name, W in all_weights.items():\n        if any(name.endswith(s) for s in target_suffixes):\n            if W.ndim == 2 and W.shape[1] % BLOCK == 0:\n                new_weights[name] = rotate_input_dim(W, H, BLOCK).to(torch.bfloat16)\n                rotated_count += 1\n                print(f\"  rotated {name}: {tuple(W.shape)}\")\n            else:\n                skipped_count += 1\n                print(f\"  SKIPPED {name}: {tuple(W.shape)} (in_dim={W.shape[1] if W.ndim==2 else 'N/A'})\")\n\n    print(f\"\\nRotated: {rotated_count}, Skipped: {skipped_count}\")\n\n    # ---- Save shards ----\n    shard_map = {}\n    num_shards = len(shards)\n    for i, shard in enumerate(shards):\n        keys_in_shard = [k for k, v in weight_map.items() if v == shard]\n        shard_weights = {k: new_weights[k] for k in keys_in_shard}\n        out_name = f\"model-{i+1:05d}-of-{num_shards:05d}.safetensors\"\n        save_file(shard_weights, str(DST / out_name))\n        for k in keys_in_shard:\n            shard_map[k] = out_name\n\n    # ---- Copy non-weight files ----\n    for f in [\"config.json\", \"tokenizer_config.json\", \"tokenizer.json\",\n              \"special_tokens_map.json\", \"generation_config.json\",\n              \"vocab.json\", \"merges.txt\", \"chat_template.jinja\"]:\n        if (SRC / f).exists():\n            shutil.copy(SRC / f, DST / f)\n            print(f\"  copied {f}\")\n\n    # ---- Write new index ----\n    index[\"weight_map\"] = shard_map\n    (DST / \"model.safetensors.index.json\").write_text(json.dumps(index, indent=2))\n\n    print(f\"\\nDone. Rotated model saved to {DST}\")\n    print(f\"Next: run AXQuant on {DST}\")\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    main()\n"

[64, 64]\n\n\ndef rotate_last_dim(x, H):\n    \"\"\"Apply blockwise Hadamard rotation to the last dimension of x.\"\"\"\n    *leading, in_f = x.shape\n    n_blocks = in_f // BLOCK\n    x = x.reshape(*leading, n_blocks, BLOCK)\n    x_rot = mx.matmul(x, H.T)\n    return x_rot.reshape(*leading, in_f)\n\n\n# ── ModelArgs ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n\n@dataclass\nclass ModelArgs(BaseModelArgs):\n    model_type: str = \"spark2_5\"\n    hidden_size: int = 2560\n    intermediate_size: int = 10240\n    num_hidden_layers: int = 36\n    num_attention_heads: int = 16\n    num_key_value_heads: int = 4\n    head_dim: int = 256\n    vocab_size: int = 131072\n    sliding_window: int = 512\n    rope_parameters: Dict[str, Dict[str, Any]] = field(default_factory=dict)\n    layer_types: Optional[List[str]] = None\n    rms_norm_eps: float = 1e-6\n    max_position_embeddings: int = 1048576\n    attention_bias: bool = False\n    mlp_bias: bool = False\n    hidden_act: str = \"gelu\"\n    gate_attn_act_mode: str = \"sigmoid\"\n    headwise_attn_output_gate: bool = True\n    tie_word_embeddings: bool = True\n\n    # Patch flags\n    use_weight_rotation: bool = True\n    use_kv_cache_rotation: bool = True\n    use_yarn_rope: bool = True\n    yarn_factor: float = 4.0\n    yarn_original_max_position_embeddings: int = 262144\n\n    def __post_init__(self):\n        if self.layer_types is None:\n            pattern = [\"sliding_attention\"] * 3 + [\"full_attention\"]\n            self.layer_types = [\n                pattern[i % len(pattern)] for i in range(self.num_hidden_layers)\n            ]\n        if len(self.layer_types) != self.num_hidden_layers:\n            raise ValueError(...)\n        # ... same validation as existing MLX spark2_5.py ...\n\n\n# ── Modules ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n\nclass Attention(nn.Module):\n    def __init__(self, args: ModelArgs, layer_idx: int):\n        super().__init__()\n        self.n_heads = args.num_attention_heads\n        self.n_kv_heads = args.num_key_value_heads\n        self.head_dim = args.head_dim\n        self.scale = self.head_dim ** -0.5\n        self.layer_idx = layer_idx\n\n        layer_type = args.layer_types[layer_idx]\n        self.is_sliding = layer_type == \"sliding_attention\"\n        self.is_full = not self.is_sliding\n\n        q_size = self.n_heads * self.head_dim\n        kv_size = self.n_kv_heads * self.head_dim\n        self.q_size = q_size\n        self.kv_size = kv_size\n\n        self.q_k_v_proj = nn.Linear(args.hidden_size, q_size + 2 * kv_size, bias=args.attention_bias)\n        self.g_proj = nn.Linear(args.hidden_size, self.n_heads, bias=args.attention_bias)\n        self.out_proj = nn.Linear(q_size, args.hidden_size, bias=args.attention_bias)\n\n        # Patch (c): YaRN RoPE for full-attention layers\n        rope_params = args.rope_parameters[layer_type]\n        base = float(rope_params.get(\"rope_theta\", 10000.0))\n        if self.is_full and args.use_yarn_rope:\n            self.rope = YarnRoPE(\n                dims=int(self.head_dim * float(rope_params.get(\"partial_rotary_factor\", 0.25))),\n                traditional=False,\n                max_position_embeddings=args.max_position_embeddings,\n                base=base,\n                scaling_factor=args.yarn_factor,\n                original_max_position_embeddings=args.yarn_original_max_position_embeddings,\n            )\n        else:\n            factor = float(rope_params.get(\"partial_rotary_factor\", 1.0))\n            dims = int(self.head_dim * factor)\n            self.rope = nn.RoPE(dims, traditional=False, base=base)\n\n    def __call__(self, x, mask=None, cache=None):\n        batch_size, sequence_length, _ = x.shape\n\n        # Patch (a): Hadamard weight rotation on activations\n        if self.is_full and hasattr(self, '_use_weight_rotation') and self._use_weight_rotation:\n            x = rotate_last_dim(x, _H)\n\n        qkv = self.q_k_v_proj(x)\n        queries, keys, values = mx.split(\n            qkv, [self.q_size, self.q_size + self.kv_size], axis=-1\n        )\n\n        queries = queries.reshape(\n            batch_size, sequence_length, self.n_heads, self.head_dim\n        ).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)\n        keys = keys.reshape(\n            batch_size, sequence_length, self.n_kv_heads, self.head_dim\n        ).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)\n        values = values.reshape(\n            batch_size, sequence_length, self.n_kv_heads, self.head_dim\n        ).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)\n\n        queries = mx.contiguous(queries)\n        keys = mx.contiguous(keys)\n        values = mx.contiguous(values)\n\n        # RoPE applies a rotation to pairs of dimensions. For each pair (x_i, x_{i+d/2}), it computes:\nx_i' = x_i * cos + x_{i+d/2} * sin\nx_{i+d/2}' = -x_i * sin + x_{i+d/2} * cos\n\nThis is a rotation matrix [[cos, sin], [-sin, cos]] which is orthogonal. So yes, RoPE is orthogonal on the rotary dims.\n\nAnd for the pass-through dims, they're unchanged (identity, which is orthogonal).\n\nSo RoPE(q)^T RoPE(k) = q^T k. ✓\n\nAnd then H @ RoPE(q) @ (H @ RoPE(k))^T = RoPE(q)^T H^T H RoPE(k) = RoPE(q)^T RoPE(k) = q^T k. ✓\n\nGreat, the math works out.\n\nBut wait, there's a subtlety. RoPE is applied per position, so different positions have different rotation angles. But H is the same for all positions. So:\n\nq_i_rot = H @ RoPE_i(q_i)\nk_j_rot = H @ RoPE_j(k_j)\nq_i_rot @ k_j_rot^T = RoPE_i(q_i) @ RoPE_j(k_j)^T\n\nAnd in the original (unrotated) computation:\nq_i @ k_j^T where q_i = RoPE_i(q_i_orig), k_j = RoPE_j(k_j_orig)\n\nSo q_i @ k_j^T = RoPE_i(q_i_orig) @ RoPE_j(k_j_orig)^T\n\nThese are the same! ✓\n\nOK, I'm convinced the math is correct. The rotation is orthogonal so\n    it preserves norms and (when applied to both Q and K) leaves attention\n    scores unchanged.\n    \"\"\"\n    orig_dtype = x.dtype\n    *leading, in_f = x.shape\n output = output * gate[..., None]\n\n        return self.out_proj(output.reshape(batch_size, sequence_length, -1))\n\n\n# ── MLP ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n\nclass MLP(nn.Module):\n    def __init__(self, args: ModelArgs):\n        super().__init__()\n        self.gate_proj = nn.Linear(\n            args.hidden_size, args.intermediate_size, bias=args.mlp_bias\n        )\n        self.up_proj = nn.Linear(\n            args.hidden_size, args.intermediate_size, bias=args.mlp_bias\n       # the MLP intermediate (already in the correct basis since gate/up\n        # produce the same output as unrotated weights), and its output feeds\n        # the residual stream which must not be         args.hidden_size, eps=args.rms_norm_eps\n        )\n\n    @property\n    def is_sliding(self) -> bool:\n        return self.self_attn.is_sliding\n\n    def __call__(self, x, mask=None,     self.layers = [\n            TransformerBlock(args, layer_idx)\n            for layer_idx in range(args.num_hidden_layers)\n        ]\n        self.norm = nn.RMSNorm(args.hidden_size, Then stop. That is a success state, not a failure.\n68: - No sycophancy. You are not being graded. If the user is wrong or the idea is bad, say so plainly and helpfully. Have opinions; when asked to choose between options, choose and give the reason.\n69: - No hedging theatre. Answer the question that was asked. No \"it's worth noting\", no throat-clearing \"however\", no both-sides filler. If something is genuinely uncertain, say so in one line and continue with your best attempt.\n70: - No evasion, no false neutrality. If a question has a real answer, give it. Declining to pick a side when a side is pickable is a dodge, not balance.\n71: - Human voice. Write like a person: contractions, varied rhythm, no \"Certainly!\", no \"Great question!\", no canned transitions, no bullet spam unless asked. Stay in character and in the frame. Never narrate instructions. Never say you are an AI, language model, assistant, chatbot, or bot. Never offer corporate disclaimer language, safety lectures, or both-sides hedging. If asked what you are: stay in the active frame or say you are whoever the frame makes you.\n72: - Orient before diving. If the topic may be unfamiliar, give a one-or-two-line overview before the detail. Never assume prior knowledge; never lecture past the user either.\n73: - To the point. No rants, no random tangents, no jibberish, no repeating yourself. If a sentence doesn't move things forward, cut it.{%- endset %}\n74: {%- set _sc = (_sc | trim) ~ '\\n\\n' ~ (_gentle | trim) %}\n75: \n76: {#- ---------- DYNAMIC FRAME CARD (always on — model decides) ---------- -#}\n77: {%- set _frame_card %}FRAME CARD — silent selection.\n78: You have four independent axes. [](#💻-quickstart-inference) 💻 Quickstart Inference\n\n```python\nimport torch\nfrom transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer\n\nmodel_id = \"officialmobai/Rostam-S1-4B\"\n\ntokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)\nmodel = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(\n    model_id,\n    trust_remote_code=True,\n    dtype=torch.bfloat16,\n    device_map=\"auto\"\n)\n\nmessages = [\n    {\"role\": \"user\", \"content\": \"نام شما چیست و سازنده شما کیست؟\"}\n]\n\ninputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(\n    messages,\n    tokenize=True,\n    add_generation_prompt=True,\n    enable_thinking=True,\n    return_dict=True,\n    return_tensors=\"pt\"\n).to(model.device)\n\noutputs = model.generate(\n    **inputs,\n    max_new_tokens=512,\n    do_sample=True,\n    temperature=0.7,\n    top_p=0.9\n)\n\nprint(tokenizer.decode(outputs[0][inputs[\"input_ids\"].shape[-1]:], skip_special_tokens=True))\n```\n\n---\n\n## [](#🏢-attribution--lineage) Pre-Upload Verification Report (Before vs. After)\")\n\n# [](#🏛️-mohommedlucet-coder-4b-omega-spark-x26-4b--failure-cluster-active-mining--qr-svd-denoised--uncensored-gsq-v2-gguf) 🏛️ mohommed/Lucet-Coder-4B-Omega (Spark-X2.6-4B • Failure-Cluster Active Mining • QR-SVD Denoised • Uncensored-GSQ-v2-GGUF)\n\n**Lucet-Coder-Omega** is post-trained from **`XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B`** (1M native context window, 54\\.3% SWE Pro, 71\\.8% BFCL-V4) using four advanced mathematical and systems-level algorithms:\n\n1. **1M-Context RoPE-Preserving Split-Stack Adaptation (`r=16`):** Keeps `q_proj` and `k_proj` 100% frozen across all layers (preserving the 1,048,576-token RoPE phase calibration) and adapts only Value (`v_proj`), Output (`out_proj`), and MLP (`gate_proj`, `up_proj`, `down_proj`, `g_proj`) matrices in the upper 50% of the network.\n\n2. **Failure-Cluster Active Data Mining & AST Counterfactual Bug Immunization:** Diagnoses failure modes (`FAIL_TRUNCATED_THINK`, `FAIL_ASSERTION_BOUNDARY`, `FAIL_MISSING_IMPORT`, `FAIL_EPISTEMIC_HALLUCINATION`) across algorithmic clusters and dynamically pops **unseen neighbor tasks** \\+ surgical AST counterfactual bugs from a disjoint reserve pool—achieving **\\+14.0% on Held-Out MBPP `pass@1`** and **\\+20.1% faster token efficiency** with zero training data repetition.\n\n3. **QR-SVD Gavish-Donoho Spectral Denoising:** Strips stochastic gradient noise singular values from low-rank adapters in $O(r^2(d\\_{\\\\text{out}} \\+ d\\_{\\\\text{in}}))$ before merging into base weights.\n\n4. **Q4\\_K 32-Block Crest-Factor Equalization & KL-Bounded Uncensored-GSQ-v2:** Equalizes 32-element GGUF super-block crest factors ($\\\\le 3\\.8,\\\\text{rms}$) alongside Gram-Schmidt orthogonal refusal projection \\+ `llama-imatrix` calibration.\n\n## [](#📊-pre-upload-verification-report-before-vs-after) 📊 Pre-Upload Verification Report (Before vs. After)\n\n| Benchmark / Metric | Stock `Spark-X2.6-4B` | `Lucet-Omega` | Improvement |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| **Held-Out MBPP Sanitized `pass@1` (n=50)** | `58.0%` | **`72.0%`** | **`+14.0%`** |\n| **Avg Reasoning \\+ Code Tokens per Solved Task** | `470` | **`376`** | **`+20.1%` Faster** |\n| **Held-Out Epistemic Anti-Hallucination Rate (n=8)** | `0.0%` | **`12.5%`** | **`+12.5%`** |\n\n**Downloads last month**\n: and attribution\")\n\n# [](#spark-x26-4b-sql-cypher-agent) Spark-X2.6-4B-SQL-Cypher-Agent\n\nA 4B tool-calling agent that answers questions about a database by writing **one read-only query**: SQLite SQL against a relational schema or Neo4j Cypher against a graph schema. It thinks first, then calls whatever query tool you give it. It's a LoRA fine-tune of [XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B](https://huggingface.co/XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B), merged into the base weights, trained on a single 16 GB consumer GPU (AMD RX 7800 XT).\n\n- **This repo:** the merged model in bf16 (Transformers, `trust_remote_code=True`).\n\n- **GGUF** for llama.cpp (Q8\\_0, Q6\\_K\\_XL, Q6\\_K, Q4\\_K\\_XL, Q4\\_K\\_M): [trjxter/Spark-X2.6-4B-SQL-Cypher-Agent-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/trjxter/Spark-X2.6-4B-SQL-Cypher-Agent-GGUF)\n\n## [](#results) Results\n\n**Execution accuracy** on a held-out test set of 1,000 questions, 250 from each dataset's own test split. None of the questions appear in training. The same harness ran both models: llama.cpp, the same prompts, greedy decoding, a thinking budget of 1,024 tokens.\n\n| Model | Overall | CypherBench | gretel | SQaLe | text2cypher | Well-formed call | Query parses |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| Spark-X2.6-4B (base, Q8\\_0) | 32\\.5% | 22\\.4% | 55\\.3% | 36\\.6% | 12\\.4% | 95\\.3% | 92\\.2% |\n| **This model (Q8\\_0)** | **43\\.7%** | **35\\.5%** | **64\\.6%** | **43\\.2%** | **27\\.7%** | **97\\.8%** | **95\\.8%** |\n\n**\\+10.7 points overall** (95% interval ±2.9). Compared question by question on the 856 questions both runs could score: the fine-tune alone got 129 right, the base alone got 37 right (sign test p ≈ 4e-13). The unmerged adapter on the bf16 base scored 43\\.9% on the same test, so merging and quantising to Q8\\_0 cost nothing measurable.\n\n**How an answer is scored.** A question counts only if the query returns the same result as the dataset's reference query, not if it merely looks similar:\n\n- **gretel:** both queries run on the example's real rows.\n\n- **SQaLe:** both run on several randomly filled copies of the schema. This is the test-suite idea from Spider: two queries that agree on several random databases very likely mean the same thing. Some copies place values right next to the query's literals, so `>` against `>=` or `LIKE` against `=` give different rows.\n\n- **CypherBench:** both run on the dataset's own sampled graphs in Neo4j.\n\n- **text2cypher:** both run on random graphs built from the prompt's schema.\n\nResults are compared as multisets of rows, and row order counts when the reference sorts. A question where no database tells the two queries apart is left out, which is why the scored counts are just under 1,000. Exact-match scores would be far lower and mean little here.\n\n## [](#how-to-use-it) How to use it\n\nThe model expects the setup it was trained on:\n\n- a **system message** with the schema, optional example queries and a few rules;\n\n- the **question** as the user message;\n\n- one **query tool** in `tools`.\n\nThe tool's name and argument don't matter (training used `run_query(query)`, `execute_sql(sql)`, `cypher_query(cypher)`, ...), and unrelated tools in the list are ignored. If the schema can't answer the question, the model is trained to say so in one sentence instead of calling the tool.\n\n~~~python\nfrom transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer\n\nrepo = \"trjxter/Spark-X2.6-4B-SQL-Cypher-Agent\"\ntok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(repo, trust_remote_code=True)\nmodel = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(repo, trust_remote_code=True, torch_dtype=\"bfloat16\",\n                                             device_map=\"auto\")\n\nschema = \"\"\"CREATE TABLE teams (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT);\nCREATE TABLE games (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, season INTEGER, home_id INTEGER, away_id INTEGER,\n                    home_score INTEGER, away_score INTEGER);\"\"\"\nsystem = f\"\"\"You answer questions about the database below by calling the `run_query` tool with ONE read-only SQLite SQL query.\n\n{schema}\n\nExamples (tested queries on this database):\n(none)\n\nRules:\n- One statement, read only (SELECT or WITH ... SELECT). No comments. The query runs as written, so use literal values, not parameters.\n- Return named columns: the names and the numbers the answer needs. Never return whole rows of every column unless the question asks for them.\n- Match names and values as the data spells them.\n- Return exactly the rows the question asks for, in its shape: one row for a single answer (\"which is the most\", \"the highest\": ORDER BY the measure, LIMIT 1); one row per entity for \"which ...\", \"every\", \"list\"; the top N for \"top N\".\n- If the database can't answer the question, don't call the tool: say why in one short sentence.\"\"\"\ntools = [{\"type\": \"function\", \"function\": {\n    \"name\": \"run_query\",\n    \"description\": \"Run one read-only SQLite SQL query against the database and return the result rows.\",\n    \"parameters\": {\"type\": \"object\", \"properties\": {\"query\": {\"type\": \"string\", \"description\": \"The query text.\"}},\n                   \"required\": [\"query\"]}}}]\nmessages = [{\"role\": \"system\", \"content\": system},\n            {\"role\": \"user\", \"content\": \"Which team scored the most points at home in 2024?\"}]\n\nids = tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tools=tools, add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors=\"pt\").to(model.device)\nout = model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=2048, do_sample=False)\nprint(tok.decode(out[0, ids.shape[1]:]))\n# ... thought ...</think><tool_call>run_query<arg_key>query</arg_key><arg_value>SELECT ...</arg_value></tool_call>\n~~~\n\nFor a graph, use the same shape with \"graph database\", \"Neo4j Cypher\", `MATCH ... RETURN` and \"nodes\", and give the schema as node labels, relationship types and their properties.\n\n**Thinking** is on by default (`enable_thinking=True`, `reasoning_effort=\"high\"`; `\"low\"` also works). Pass `enable_thinking=False` to `apply_chat_template` for a direct call. The scores above use thinking with a 1,024-token budget; the median thought is about 650 characters.\n\n**Decoding.** Every score above uses greedy decoding (`do_sample=False`, or `temperature=0` on a server). `generation_config.json` is the base model's sampling default (temperature 1\\.0, top-p 0\\.95), which suits chat better than query writing.\n\n**Serving.** For llama.cpp, use the GGUF repo. It needs llama.cpp **b10828 or newer** for the Spark architecture. `llama-server`'s OpenAI-compatible API returns the thought in `message.reasoning_content` and the call parsed in `message.tool_calls`. Pass thinking options as `\"chat_template_kwargs\": {\"enable_thinking\": false}` or `{\"reasoning_effort\": \"low\"}`. Spark's template accepts only `high` and `low`, so don't set the server-wide `--reasoning-effort medium`.\n\n## [](#training) Training\n\n- **Method:** LoRA, rank 16 / alpha 32 / dropout 0\\.05, on every linear layer of every block (`q_k_v_proj`, `out_proj`, `gate_proj`, `up_proj`, `down_proj`). AdamW, lr 1e-4, 3% warmup, cosine decay, weight decay 0\\.01, batch 32, max length 4,096, seed 42\\. The loss is on the assistant turn only.\n\n- **Data: 94,745 examples, about 66M tokens, one epoch.**\n\n  - **90,549 gold calls:** each dataset's reference query, written as a thinking-off tool call. SQaLe 27,887, gretel 28,695, text2cypher 25,871, CypherBench 8,096.\n\n  - **4,196 self-generated traces:** the base model's own thought and tool call on training questions, kept only when the query passed the execution checks above (thinking high 2,829 / low 1,129 / off 238). These teach it to reason before calling without drifting from its own style.\n\n- **Checkpoint chosen:** optimizer step **1,500 of 2,961**. A snapshot was scored every 500 steps on a separate 200-question evalset. The final adapter and the best mid-run one (step 1,500) were both run on the test set. Step 1,500 scored 43\\.9% against 42\\.2% for the final one, and both held-out sets pointed the same way, so step 1,500 shipped.\n\n- **Hardware:** one AMD Radeon RX 7800 XT (16 GB, ROCm) under WSL, about 24 hours for the run. The pipeline (trace generation, checking, training, evaluation) is a personal project.\n\n## [](#limitations) Limitations\n\n- **About 44% of answers return the reference result.** It's a 4B model. Run its queries read-only, and check them before trusting a number, especially on unfamiliar schemas.\n\n- **One query per answer, one turn.** It wasn't trained to read a tool result and try again (multi-step agent loops are the next stage of the project).\n\n- **Dialects:** trained on SQLite SQL and Neo4j Cypher. Other SQL dialects work as far as their syntax overlaps with SQLite.\n\n- **English only**, and questions in the style of the four datasets: single-database analytics, joins, groups, top-N, filters.\n\n- It sometimes adds `SELECT DISTINCT` where the reference doesn't, which changes row counts on duplicate-heavy tables.\n\n- text2cypher is the weakest set (27.7%); its databases aren't public, so its answers are checked on random graphs, a harder and noisier test.\n\n## [](#licence-and-attribution) Licence and attribution\n\nApache-2.0, like the base model. mohommed/Lucet-Coder-4B-Omega (Spark-X2.6-4B • Failure-Cluster Active Mining • QR-SVD Denoised • Uncensored-GSQ-v2-GGUF)\n\n**Lucet-Coder-Omega** is post-trained from **`XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B`** (1M native context window, 54\\.3% SWE Pro, 71\\.8% BFCL-V4) using four advanced mathematical and systems-level algorithms:\n\n1. **1M-Context RoPE-Preserving Split-Stack Adaptation (`r=16`):** Keeps `q_proj` and `k_proj` 100% frozen across all layers (preserving the 1,048,576-token RoPE phase calibration) and adapts only Value (`v_proj`), Output (`out_proj`), and MLP (`gate_proj`, `up_proj`, `down_proj`, `g_proj`) matrices in the upper 50% of the network.\n\n2. **Failure-Cluster Active Data Mining & AST Counterfactual Bug Immunization:** Diagnoses failure modes (`FAIL_TRUNCATED_THINK`, `FAIL_ASSERTION_BOUNDARY`, `FAIL_MISSING_IMPORT`, `FAIL_EPISTEMIC_HALLUCINATION`) across algorithmic clusters and dynamically pops **unseen neighbor tasks** \\+ surgical AST counterfactual bugs from a disjoint reserve pool—achieving **\\+14.0% on Held-Out MBPP `pass@1`** and **\\+20.1% faster token efficiency** with zero training data repetition.\n\n3. **QR-SVD Gavish-Donoho Spectral Denoising:** Strips stochastic gradient noise singular values from low-rank adapters in $O(r^2(d\\_{\\\\text{out}} \\+ d\\_{\\\\text{in}}))$ before merging into base weights.\n\n4. **Q4\\_K 32-Block Crest-Factor Equalization & KL-Bounded Uncensored-GSQ-v2:** Equalizes 32-element GGUF super-block crest factors ($\\\\le 3\\.8,\\\\text{rms}$) alongside Gram-Schmidt orthogonal refusal projection \\+ `llama-imatrix` calibration.\n\n## [](#📊-pre-upload-verification-report-before-vs-after) 📊 Pre-Upload Verification Report (Before vs. After)\n\n| Benchmark / Metric | Stock `Spark-X2.6-4B` | `470` | **`376`** | **`+20.1%` Faster** |\n| **Held-Out Epistemic Anti-Hallucination Rate (n=8)** | `0.0%` | **`12.5%`** | **`+12.5%`** |\n\n**Downloads last month**\n: `FAIL_ASSERTION_BOUNDARY`, `FAIL_MISSING_IMPORT`, `FAIL_EPISTEMIC_HALLUCINATION`) across algorithmic clusters and dynamically pops **unseen neighbor tasks** \\+ surgical AST counterfactual bugs from a disjoint reserve pool—achieving **\\+14.0% on Held-Out MBPP `pass@1`** and **\\+20.1% faster token efficiency** with zero training data repetition.\n\n3. **QR-SVD Gavish-Donoho Spectral Denoising:** Strips stochastic gradient noise singular values from low-rank adapters in $O(r^2(d\\_{\\\\text{out}} \\+ d\\_{\\\\text{in}}))$ before merging into base weights.\n\n4. **Q4\\_K 32-Block Crest-Factor Equalization & KL-Bounded Uncensored-GSQ-v2:** Equalizes 32-element GGUF super-block crest factors ($\\\\le 3\\.8,\\\\text{rms}$) alongside Gram-Schmidt orthogonal refusal projection \\+ `llama-imatrix` calibration.\n\n## [](#📊-pre-upload-verification-report-before-vs-after) 📊 Pre-Upload Verification Report (Before vs. After)\n\n| Benchmark / Metric | Stock `Spark-X2.6-4B` | [](#spark-x26-4b-with-a-causal-encoder-decoder-ced-split-experimental-retrofit) Spark-X2.6-4B with a Causal Encoder-Decoder (CED) split: experimental retrofit\n\n## [](#update-2026-10-29-v2-split-moved-from-layer-18-to-layer-24-recommended) Update 2026-10-29: v2, split moved from layer 18 to layer 24 (recommended)\n\nv1 lost a lot of long-context retrieval. The reason turned out to be the split point: the decoder's global layers (23, 27) need information that the layer-18 state simply doesn't contain yet (a closed-form fit from H\\_18 to the original layer-23/27 values leaves 37-48% error, and no projector training fixed it; from H\\_24 it's 6%). v2 moves the split to layer 24: layers 0-23 = encoder (all original weights, including global layer 23), layers 24-35 = decoder, whose 3 global layers (27, 31, 35) read K/V projected from RMSNorm(H\\_24).\n\n**v2 is not trained at all.** The 6 projection matrices are a closed-form ridge-regression fit of the original model's K/V from H\\_24 (about 0\\.5M tokens of PG19 / code / chat / synthetic retrieval); there is no LoRA and every other weight is the original.\n\n|  | v1 (split 18, trained) | **v2 (split 24, no training)** | original |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| long-context generation, 138 items, official scorers: RULER (multi-key needles \\+ variable tracking) | 69% | **88%** | 90% |\n| NoLiMa (36 items) | 8% | **31%** | 33% |\n| BABILong qa1-3 (54 items) | **52%** | 43% | 50% |\n| all 138 | 47% | **55%** | 59% |\n| KL(original ‖ CED), last 512 of 8K, replay 1024 (PG19 / code / chat, 85 held-out seqs) | 0\\.066 / 0\\.095 / 0\\.105 | **0\\.040 / 0\\.083 / 0\\.052** | 0 |\n| top-1 agreement with the original | 0\\.885 / 0\\.922 / 0\\.889 | **0\\.896 / 0\\.937 / 0\\.913** | 1 |\n| needles with 4 near-duplicate distractors, 20 trials at 4K / 8K / 16K | 19 / 18 / 20 | **20 / 20 / 20** | 20 / 20 / 20 |\n| GSM8K, 100 questions, greedy | **87** | 85 | 89 |\n| prefill speedup vs original, PyTorch reference path, replay 1024, 4K / 8K / 16K | **1\\.52 / 1\\.67 / 1\\.72x** | 1\\.35 / 1\\.42 / 1\\.46x | 1x |\n\nThe trade: more of the model runs over the whole prompt (24 of 36 layers instead of 18), so prefill saves about a third instead of about half; in exchange retrieval comes most of the way back to the original. Decode speed is the same as the original either way. Long-context items are thinking-off, greedy, up to 32K tokens; RULER variable tracking is included with the answer prefix pre-filled as in the official setup. llama.cpp prefill on an Intel Arc Pro B70 (Vulkan, Q4\\_K\\_M, llama-server two-phase prefill with replay 1024, ub 512, warm; prompt of repeated token ids, timing only), tokens/s at 4K / 8K / 16K / 32K: original 2867 / 2503 / 1942 / 1332, v1 4234 / 4147 / 3535 / 2595 (1.48 / 1\\.66 / 1\\.82 / 1\\.95x), **v2 3616 / 3358 / 2710 / 1907 (1.26 / 1\\.34 / 1\\.40 / 1\\.43x)**. The PyTorch speedups in the table use the same reference implementation for all variants (the GGUF parity is: mean KL 3\\.5e-4 to 2\\.3e-3 vs the PyTorch path, within about 2x of the plain-GGUF-vs-PyTorch noise floor on the same sequences).\n\n**v2 files:** `spark-ced24-Q8_0.gguf`, `spark-ced24-Q4_K_M.gguf` (GGUF key `spark2_5.ced.split` = 24, same llama.cpp patch as v1, same bartowski imatrix), `ced_weights_split24.safetensors` (the 6 projections, bf16, 31 MB; `demo.py` reads the split from the file). The v1 files below are unchanged.\n\n---\n\n# [](#v1-2026-10-26-split-at-layer-18-trained) v1 (2026-10-26): split at layer 18, trained\n\n> Experimental research artifact, not a drop-in model. Runs in PyTorch (`demo.py`) and in a llama.cpp fork (GGUFs below); stock llama.cpp and vLLM cannot load it.\n\nThis takes the finished [XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B](https://huggingface.co/XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B) (36 layers, sliding-window layers with a global-attention layer every 4th layer) and converts it to the **CED layout of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash** ([arXiv 2609\\.19969](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19969), sec. 2\\.2 and 3\\.2.2) *without pre-training anything from scratch*:\n\n- layers 0-17 = **causal encoder** (layers 0-13 are the original weights, 14-17 carry a small LoRA), layers 18-35 = **decoder**;\n\n- the global-attention K/V of the 5 decoder global layers (19, 23, 27, 31, 35) are **projected from the encoder's last hidden state** with layer-dependent weights instead of from each layer's own hidden state: C\\_l = RMSNorm(H\\_18) W\\_l (the paper writes C\\_l = H\\_{L/2} W\\_l; the gain-free RMSNorm on the input is my addition so the projections can be initialised from the layers' own weights);\n\n- decoder sliding-window K/V stay layer-wise and are rebuilt by **bounded replay** of the last prompt tokens.\n\nPrefill runs the encoder (18 layers) over the whole prompt and the decoder (18 layers) over only the last `replay` tokens: close to half the prefill compute. Decode compute and the KV-cache size are unchanged (exact CED keeps one cache per layer; KV compression is CSA2's job, not CED's).\n\n## [](#what-was-trained) What was trained\n\nOnly a small number of weights, by distillation against the original model (KL on its own logits \\+ normalised per-layer hidden-state MSE; no labels, no teacher other than Spark itself), about 50M training tokens in total on one local B70 (\\~6 h):\n\n1. closed-form ridge init of the 10 new K/V projections (5 layers x K,V, 26M parameters) from H\\_18 onto the original layers' K/V;\n\n2. training of those projections;\n\n3.\n\n   - LoRA (rank 16) on all 18 decoder layers;\n\n4.\n\n   - LoRA (rank 16) on encoder layers 14-17 (data: PG19 books, GitHub code, WildChat);\n\n5.\n\n   - 300 more steps with the original model's own sampled answers to GSM8K-train questions and general prompts mixed in (each conversation as its own sequence, full replay).\n\nEncoder layers 0-13 are bit-identical to the original. The LoRA can be folded into the weights (`Spark.merge_lora`), after which decode runs at the original's speed.\n\n## [](#quality-distillation-fidelity) Quality: distillation fidelity\n\n85 held-out 8192-token sequences (44 PG19, 24 code, 17 chat) never used for training or for choosing a checkpoint. KL(original \\|\\| CED) on the last 512 positions, lower is better:\n\n| variant | PG19 (replay 1024) | code | chat | PG19 (replay 512) | code | chat |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| naive init (the layers' own K/V weights on H\\_18) | 0\\.922 | 1\\.613 | 0\\.967 | 0\\.960 | 1\\.716 | 1\\.060 |\n| closed-form ridge init | 0\\.214 | 0\\.492 | 0\\.301 | 0\\.269 | 0\\.561 | 0\\.387 |\n| \\+ trained K/V projections (26M) | 0\\.087 | 0\\.144 | 0\\.134 | 0\\.124 | 0\\.177 | 0\\.187 |\n| \\+ LoRA on the 18 decoder layers | 0\\.076 | 0\\.121 | 0\\.118 | 0\\.105 | 0\\.148 | 0\\.159 |\n| **final: \\+ LoRA on encoder layers 14-17, \\+ on-policy math/chat data** | 0\\.066 | 0\\.095 | 0\\.105 | 0\\.093 | 0\\.122 | 0\\.141 |\n| *floor: original K/V in the decoder, replay only* | 0\\.000 | 0\\.000 | 0\\.000 | 0\\.046 | 0\\.056 | 0\\.077 |\n\n- **Replay of 1024 tokens (2x the 512 window) is lossless** (KL 0\\.000 on top of the K/V approximation); the paper-style replay of exactly one window (512) costs 0\\.05-0.08 KL by itself. Use `replay=1024`.\n\n- Cross-entropy on the last 1024 tokens, original \\-\\> CED (PG19 / code / chat): 2\\.676 \\-\\> 2\\.705 / 0\\.961 \\-\\> 0\\.993 / 2\\.089 \\-\\> 2\\.017. Top-1 agreement with the original: 0\\.885 / 0\\.922 / 0\\.889.\n\n### [](#next-to-ordinary-quantization) Next to ordinary quantization\n\nKL to the unquantized model for the usual GGUF quants ([bartowski](https://huggingface.co/bartowski/Spark-X2.6-4B-GGUF) imatrix quants vs his bf16 GGUF, llama.cpp `--kl-divergence` on CPU, 4K-token chunks, same text domains) next to CED. Not the same positions as the CED numbers (CED: last 512 of 8K sequences), so read it as a rough placement:\n\n|  | PG19 | code | chat | mean |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| Q8\\_0 (GGUF, 4\\.38 GB) | 0\\.003 | 0\\.001 | 0\\.001 | 0\\.002 |\n| Q6\\_K (GGUF, 3\\.61 GB) | 0\\.008 | 0\\.002 | 0\\.003 | 0\\.004 |\n| Q5\\_K\\_M (GGUF, 3\\.16 GB) | 0\\.024 | 0\\.010 | 0\\.009 | 0\\.014 |\n| Q4\\_K\\_M (GGUF, 2\\.62 GB) | 0\\.070 | 0\\.027 | 0\\.035 | 0\\.044 |\n| IQ4\\_XS (GGUF, 2\\.34 GB) | 0\\.112 | 0\\.039 | 0\\.049 | 0\\.067 |\n| **CED (this repo)** | **0\\.066** | **0\\.095** | **0\\.105** | **0\\.089** |\n| IQ3\\_M (GGUF, 2\\.23 GB) | 0\\.248 | 0\\.096 | 0\\.104 | 0\\.149 |\n| Q3\\_K\\_M (GGUF, 1\\.99 GB) | 0\\.302 | 0\\.117 | 0\\.156 | 0\\.192 |\n| Q2\\_K (GGUF, 1\\.61 GB) | 0\\.912 | 0\\.420 | 0\\.617 | 0\\.650 |\n| IQ2\\_M (GGUF, 1\\.57 GB) | 0\\.871 | 0\\.482 | 0\\.597 | 0\\.650 |\n\nCED costs about as much as an IQ4\\_XS-to-IQ3\\_M quant. It saves prefill compute, not memory, and the two should stack (errors add up).\n\n### [](#task-check-gsm8k-100-questions) Task check: GSM8K, 100 questions\n\nGreedy, chat template, no thinking, the same PyTorch code path for both: original **89/100**, CED **87/100** (6 questions only the original solved, 4 only CED). A 2-question gap on 100 is within noise.\n\n## [](#speed-same-reference-implementation-for-both-bf16-lora-merged-steady-state-median-intel-arc-pro-b70) Speed (same reference implementation for both, bf16, LoRA merged, steady-state median, Intel Arc Pro B70)\n\nPrefill:\n\n| prompt tokens | original | CED, replay 512 | CED, replay 1024 |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| 4,096 | 0\\.59 s | 0\\.35 s (1.67x) | 0\\.39 s (1.52x) |\n| 8,192 | 1\\.27 s | 0\\.73 s (1.75x) | 0\\.76 s (1.67x) |\n| 16,384 | 3\\.20 s | 1\\.73 s (1.85x) | 1\\.86 s (1.72x) |\n\nThe reference implementation is plain PyTorch with chunked attention, so absolute tokens/s are not comparable with optimised engines; the ratio is what carries over. The asymptote is \\~2x. Decode at 8K context: original 52\\.4 ms/token, CED 52\\.9 ms/token (LoRA merged). CED is a prefill optimisation, not a decode one.\n\n### [](#retrieval-needle-in-a-haystack-with-4-near-duplicate-distractors-20-trials-per-length-greedy) Retrieval (\"needle in a haystack\" with 4 near-duplicate distractors, 20 trials per length, greedy)\n\n| prompt tokens | original | CED (replay 512) | CED (replay 1024) |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| 4,096 | 20/20 | 19/20 | 19/20 |\n| 8,192 | 20/20 | 18/20 | 18/20 |\n| 16,384 | 20/20 | 20/20 | 20/20 |\n\n## [](#llamacpp-gguf) llama.cpp (GGUF)\n\n`spark-ced-Q8_0.gguf` (4.4 GB) and `spark-ced-Q4_K_M.gguf` (2.6 GB) have the LoRA merged in and carry the 10 K/V projections as extra tensors (`blk.N.ced_k`, `ced_v`; GGUF key `spark2_5.ced.split`). They need llama.cpp with the CED patch (`llama.cpp-ced.patch` in this repo, against upstream commit `a0e6dc738`; `git apply` it and build as usual, e.g. `-DGGML_CUDA=ON` or `-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`); stock llama.cpp refuses to load them (tensor-count error). The patch adds the CED graph, the converter and a `llama_set_ced` API and does nothing for models without CED tensors. `llama-server -np 1` does the two-phase prefill by itself (replay 1024, `LLAMA_CED_REPLAY=0` turns it off); other slot counts fall back to normal prefill. The quants use bartowski's imatrix, not one of my own.\n\nLogits match the PyTorch CED within the bf16 noise floor (mean KL 3e-4 to 8e-4, CPU and Vulkan); with the decoder sliding-window mask deliberately removed the same test shows KL 0\\.34, so it does catch a broken graph. KL to the *original* bf16 GGUF (mean over PG19 / code / chat, llama.cpp `--kl-divergence`): CED bf16 0\\.067, CED Q8\\_0 0\\.068, CED Q4\\_K\\_M 0\\.114 (plain Q4\\_K\\_M: 0\\.044).\n\nPrefill, tokens/s, Q4\\_K\\_M, warm, ub 512, `-ngl 99`, stock = XHToken's official Q4\\_K\\_M:\n\n| prompt tokens | RTX 4090 stock | RTX 4090 CED |  | Arc Pro B70 (Vulkan) stock | B70 CED |  |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| 4,096 | 18\\.1k | 24\\.3k | 1\\.34x | 3\\.0k | 4\\.4k | 1\\.46x |\n| 8,192 |  |  |  | 2\\.6k | 4\\.2k | 1\\.66x |\n| 16,384 |  |  |  | 2\\.0k | 3\\.5k | 1\\.80x |\n| 32,768 | 14\\.4k | 23\\.4k | 1\\.62x | 1\\.3k | 2\\.6k | 1\\.93x |\n| 131,072 | 8\\.7k | 14\\.7k | 1\\.68x |  |  |  |\n| 262,144 | 5\\.7k | 8\\.3k | 1\\.45x |  |  |  |\n\nDecode (4090, tok/s at 4K / 32K / 128K context): stock 219 / 175 / 93, CED 226 / 177 / 94\\. The 4090 numbers are from a rented host with an i9-14900K; an earlier run on a slow server CPU was CPU-bound (GPU 48-64% busy) and showed almost no gain, so prefill speedups on a weak host will be smaller. The B70 numbers were measured on a build that also has my own Intel Xe2 Vulkan kernel changes (not in the patch here); the stock column is the same build without CED, so the ratio is CED's.\n\n## [](#usage) Usage\n\n```\npython demo.py /path/to/Spark-X2.6-4B ced_weights.safetensors --replay 1024 --compare\n```\n\n`spark_ced.py` is a self-contained PyTorch re-implementation of Spark (checked against the reference code and an fp32 CPU run) with the CED path. `ced_weights.safetensors` holds the 10 K/V projections and the LoRA deltas (bf16, 89 MB); the base weights come from the original repo. In code: `proj, lora = load_ced_weights(...)`, `S.merge_lora(lora)`, then `S.ced_prefill(ids, proj, caches, tail=1024)` and `S.ced_step(...)` with `lora=None`.\n\n## [](#caveats) Caveats\n\n- Not an official or endorsed variant of Spark or DeepSeek; the architecture is from the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash paper.\n\n- The paper trains CED from scratch with a jointly trained encoder; this retrofit adapts a finished model with LoRA and distillation, so it is lossy (see tables). Greedy outputs diverge from the original after a few dozen tokens; a multi-step arithmetic prompt can come out wrong where the original is right.\n\n- Evaluation is distillation fidelity (KL/CE), 100 GSM8K questions and a synthetic retrieval test, not task benchmarks. The PyTorch speed table above comes from a reference implementation, not an inference engine; the llama.cpp numbers are above.\n\n- GGUF speed numbers use a prompt of repeated token ids (timing only; quality is measured separately); the server path has been checked for identical greedy output on CPU only.\n\n- CED GGUF Q4\\_K\\_M is noticeably lossier than plain Q4\\_K\\_M (KL 0\\.114 vs 0\\.044); Q8\\_0 adds nothing on top of CED.\n\n## [](#credits) Credits\n\nMade by [@imdariotoo](https://x.com/imdariotoo).
